paragraphs.heading: What pumice is
paragraphs.text: Pumice is a volcanic rock made of rough-textured volcanic glass that is extremely vesicular. It may or may not contain crystals, and it is typically light-colored. It is an igneous rock with a foamy look. The name comes from the Latin word pumex, which is related to the Latin spuma, meaning foam. In powdered or dust form it is called pumicite.

paragraphs.heading: How the foam forms
paragraphs.text: Pumice is made when super-heated rock under high pressure is thrown rapidly out of a volcano. Its foamy form comes from two things happening at once: rapid cooling and a rapid drop in pressure. The pressure drop lowers how much gas, including water and CO₂, can stay dissolved in the lava, so the gases come out quickly as bubbles. The same thing happens when a carbonated drink is opened and bubbles of CO₂ appear. The cooling and the pressure drop together freeze the bubbles in place.

paragraphs.heading: A rock that floats
paragraphs.text: Pumice has a porosity of 64–85% by volume. It floats on water, perhaps for years, and sinks only once it is waterlogged. When pumice from an underwater eruption reaches the surface, it can form pumice rafts that can be a hazard for ships. After Krakatoa exploded, rafts of pumice stayed adrift in the Indian Ocean for as long as 20 years, and tree trunks floated among them. In 1979, 1984 and 2006, underwater eruptions near Tonga made large rafts that floated hundreds of kilometres to Fiji. Pumice rafts also disperse and support several marine species.

paragraphs.heading: Colour and makeup
paragraphs.text: Pumice is commonly pale. Its colours run from white, cream, blue or gray through to green-brown or black. A black colour comes from magnetite, a black iron oxide mineral, whose tiny crystals are scattered through the pumice. Black pumice can be confused with black scoria. In composition pumice is commonly, though not only, silicic or felsic to intermediate, and it is never mafic.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of bubble
paragraphs.text: The bubbles, called vesicles, come in two main forms. Most pumice contains tube-shaped microvesicles, which can give it a silky or fibrous fabric. The other form is spherical or nearly so and results from high vapor pressure during an eruption. One kind of pumice, called tube pumice or woody pumice, can closely resemble wood.

paragraphs.heading: Pumice and scoria
paragraphs.text: Scoria is another vesicular volcanic rock. It differs from pumice in having larger vesicles and thicker vesicle walls, and in being dark-colored and denser. Scoria often sinks, though not always. The magma that forms scoria has a lower viscosity, and that is what produces the difference.
